title: This Fossil Captures the Final Moments of a T. Rex Attack
hook: A Tyrannosaurus tooth is still embedded in its prey's skull — rare direct fossil evidence of exactly how the giant carnivore hunted.
key_points: A fossilized Edmontosaurus skull was found with a Tyrannosaurus tooth still embedded in its face.
This is rare direct physical evidence of a specific predator-prey encounter, rather than behavior inferred from bone shape alone.
The bite's location and force suggest Tyrannosaurus delivered an incredibly powerful face-to-face bite.
The find offers a concrete data point for reconstructing how Tyrannosaurus actually attacked its prey.
content_html: Most of what we know about how Tyrannosaurus hunted comes from skeletal anatomy and educated guesswork. This fossil is the real thing: a tooth still lodged in its victim's face.
extra_html: Paleontologists recovered a fossilized Edmontosaurus skull with a Tyrannosaurus tooth embedded directly in it — rare direct evidence of an actual predation event, rather than behavior inferred from bone shape or bite-mark statistics. The location and apparent force of the bite suggest Tyrannosaurus delivered an incredibly powerful face-to-face strike, offering a rare, concrete data point for reconstructing how the largest predator of its era actually attacked its prey.

related.title: T. rex Took 40 Years to Reach Full Size
related.hook: We picture T. rex bulking up fast. A study of 17 fossils says the opposite: the eight-ton predator may have taken about 40 years to reach full size — a slow, decades-long build.

related.title: The Cambrian Explosion
related.hook: Around 540 million years ago, after billions of years of mostly microbes, animal life suddenly diversified into a riot of body plans — most major groups appearing in a geological blink.

flashcards.prompt: What makes this fossil unusual compared to most evidence about T. rex hunting?
flashcards.back_html: It's direct physical evidence of one specific attack — a Tyrannosaurus tooth still embedded in its prey's skull — rather than behavior inferred from skeletal anatomy alone.

flashcards.prompt: What does the fossil suggest about how Tyrannosaurus attacked?

choices.text: It delivered an incredibly powerful face-to-face bite
It only attacked prey from behind
It rarely made physical contact with its prey

flashcards.explanation_html: The bite's location, directly in the prey's face, and its apparent force point to a powerful frontal attack rather than an ambush from behind.
